text_blocks.snippet: A diagnosis of Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) can only be definitively made through a post-mortem examination of the brain. While living individuals can exhibit symptoms consistent with CTE, doctors can't confirm the presence of CTE until after death. Instead, doctors use a process of elimination, ruling out other conditions with similar symptoms to arrive at a potential diagnosis.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: CTE symptoms can include memory loss, confusion, impaired judgment, impulse control problems, aggression, depression, anxiety, suicidality, parkinsonism, and progressive dementia. These symptoms often appear years or even decades after the last brain trauma.

list.title: Early Symptoms:
list.snippet: Early signs may involve mood disturbances like depression, anxiety, and aggression, as well as difficulty with impulse control.

list.title: Later Symptoms:
list.snippet: Later stages can include memory and thinking problems, potentially leading to dementia.

list.title: Diagnosis Process:
list.snippet: Doctors will assess a person's history of head injuries and rule out other conditions like Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease. Brain scans like MRI and CT scans can be used to look for structural changes, but they may not always show the specific patterns associated with CTE. Spinal taps to test cerebrospinal fluid may also be used.

list.title: Definitive Diagnosis:
list.snippet: The only way to confirm CTE is through a neuropathological examination of the brain tissue after death, which involves identifying the abnormal tau protein deposits characteristic of CTE, according to a YouTube video from a medical channel.

text_blocks.snippet: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) is a progressive brain disease linked to repeated head trauma, often experienced by athletes in contact sports or individuals with a history of head injuries. It is characterized by a range of symptoms, including cognitive decline, mood and behavioral changes, and eventually, dementia. Currently, CTE can only be definitively diagnosed after death through brain examination, but suspected or probable CTE can be diagnosed based on symptoms and history.
snippet_highlighted_words: a progressive brain disease linked to repeated head trauma, often experienced by athletes in contact sports or individuals with a history of head injuries

list.title: Cause:
list.snippet: Repeated head trauma, including concussions and subconcussive hits, is the primary cause.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: CTE symptoms can include memory loss, confusion, aggression, depression, impaired judgment, and changes in behavior. As the disease progresses, symptoms can worsen and lead to dementia.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: While definitive diagnosis requires post-mortem examination of the brain, doctors can diagnose suspected or probable CTE based on a person's history, symptoms, and neurological exams.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Currently, there is no cure for CTE, but treatments are available to manage symptoms and improve quality of life.
Contact sports: Football, boxing, hockey, and other sports with repeated head impacts are associated with increased risk.
Military service: Blast injuries and other head trauma can increase the risk.
Other trauma: Physical assault and other activities involving repeated head impacts can also contribute.

text_blocks.snippet: Importance of Early Detection and Management:

While CTE can only be definitively diagnosed after death, early recognition of symptoms is crucial for individuals with a history of head trauma. Early intervention with therapies and support can help manage symptoms and improve the overall well-being of those affected.

Ongoing research aims to better understand the mechanisms of CTE, identify biomarkers for early diagnosis, and develop effective treatments. Advances in brain imaging, such as MRI and PET scans, offer hope for more accurate and earlier diagnosis in the future, according to Harvard Health.
